rows.selection_reason: No experiments are completed yet, so the key uncertainty is whether RNA alone provides a useful signal and what baseline performance to use for later comparisons. config_001 tests the simplest RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline, isolating the RNA modality and a standard representation without adding aggregation or fusion. It is the best next experiment because it is low-complexity, gives a reference point for evaluating multiprofile aggregation, learned RNA encoders, image-only models, and multimodal fusion under a limited budget.

The only completed result is a weak RNA-only PCA single-profile baseline (accuracy 0.485, F1 0.464), so it is still unclear whether image data adds useful signal. config_010 tests an image-only ResNet50 single-profile baseline, isolating the value of the image representation without introducing aggregation or fusion complexity. This reduces uncertainty about whether image information is worth pursuing before investing further in multimodal or multiprofile configurations.

RNA-only PCA singleprofile is much stronger than image-only ResNet singleprofile (0.485 vs 0.208 accuracy; F1 0.464 vs 0.172), so the RNA branch is the most promising current direction. config_002 keeps the same modality and RNA encoder but tests multiprofile with simple avgpool, clarifying whether multiple profiles add useful information over the singleprofile baseline without adding transformer complexity or a new modality. This is an efficient exploitation of the strongest evidence and creates a multiprofile RNA anchor for later aggregation, encoder, or multimodal comparisons.

RNA-only multiprofile PCA with avgpool (config_002) is the strongest result so far, clearly outperforming single-profile RNA and image-only ResNet. The main uncertainty is whether transformer aggregation over multiple profiles improves on simple avgpool. config_003 changes only the aggregation method, isolating that effect and extending the most promising RNA design before adding more complex encoders or multimodal fusion.

The strongest evidence so far is RNA-only PCA with multiprofile avgpool, which substantially outperforms single-profile PCA and transformer aggregation, while image-only ResNet is weak. The key uncertainty is whether a learned RNA encoder can improve on PCA under this best-known profile and aggregation setting. config_005 keeps profile_setting=multiprofile and aggregation=avgpool fixed and changes only the RNA encoder to scvi_n200, isolating the representation effect. This is the best next use of budget because it either confirms PCA is sufficient or identifies a better RNA representation before adding multimodal complexity.

The strongest completed result is RNA-only multiprofile with scvi_n200 and avgpool (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1), and avgpool beat transformer for PCA multiprofile (0.591 vs 0.519), but that aggregation comparison is based on only one encoder. config_006 keeps the promising multiprofile + scvi_n200 setting and changes only aggregation to transformer, directly testing whether the transformer penalty persists with a stronger RNA encoder. This is a clean one-factor extension of the current best direction, reduces uncertainty about aggregation before investing in more complex multimodal settings, and may either confirm avgpool or reveal a competitive transformer configuration.

Existing evidence shows RNA-only models strongly outperform image-only models, multiprofile aggregation improved PCA-based RNA, and scvi_n200 multiprofile models are currently the best performers with validation accuracy around 0.65 and F1 around 0.63. However, there is no singleprofile scvi_n200 result, so it is unclear whether the multiprofile gain is specific to PCA or also holds for the stronger scvi representation. config_004 tests the simpler singleprofile scvi_n200 baseline, isolating the effect of profile setting and aggregation for the currently most promising RNA encoder. This is the best next experiment because it exploits the strong scvi RNA direction without adding a new encoder or modality, clarifies whether multiprofile complexity is necessary, and provides a cleaner basis for later multimodal or fusion comparisons.

Existing evidence shows multiprofile RNA with scvi is the strongest direction (0.650-0.653 validation accuracy), and avgpool is the more reliable aggregation: it is clearly better for PCA and nearly tied for scvi. scgpt is an untested RNA representation. This experiment tests whether scgpt improves over scvi while holding profile setting and aggregation constant, isolating the effect of representation. It is the best next use of budget because it has high expected performance, directly extends the strongest RNA-only evidence, and avoids relying on the small transformer advantage or jumping to a confounded multimodal fusion test before establishing the best RNA encoder.

Image evidence is sparse: the only image experiment so far, config_010 with resnet50 singleprofile, is weak (0.208 accuracy), so it is unclear whether the image modality lacks useful signal or whether the image encoder is simply too weak. config_013 tests this by replacing resnet50 with imagenet_vit_l while keeping singleprofile and no fusion, isolating the effect of image representation. This is the best next experiment under a limited budget because it gives a clean comparison to config_010 and determines whether a stronger image encoder is worth adding to multimodal fusion before spending budget on more complex multiprofile or fused configurations.

The strongest evidence is that RNA-only scvi_n200 with multiprofile is much better than image-only models, with config_005 and config_006 reaching about 0.65 validation accuracy and F1, while image-only models are only around 0.21-0.23. The key uncertainty is whether image features can complement the strong RNA representation at all. config_036 tests this directly by extending the strong scvi_n200 multiprofile avgpool RNA baseline with the slightly better single-image encoder, imagenet_vit_l, and a simple concat fusion. This keeps the RNA encoder, profile setting, and aggregation fixed, making it a clean first multimodal test: if it improves over the RNA-only baseline, it justifies further fusion and image-encoder experiments; if not, it argues against investing more budget in complex multimodal variants.
